chapter.title: Plato and Aristotle: is the real world the one we see?

cards.body: Socrates has just been carried out of the dinner, executed in 399 BC. His student Plato takes the chair and talks for 40 years. Then Plato's own student, Aristotle, who sat at that table for about 20 years, leans in and says: teacher, I think you have it backwards. This chapter is that one exchange.
cards.simpler: Socrates was put to death in 399 BC. His student Plato then taught for about 40 years. Plato's own student, Aristotle, sat in that classroom for about 20 years. Then he spoke up and said his teacher had things backwards. **This chapter is that one disagreement**, between a teacher and his best student, about where the real world is.

cards.title: The cave
cards.body:
Plato tells a story in his book the Republic. Picture prisoners chained in a cave since birth, facing a wall. Behind them a fire burns, and people carry puppets past it, so shadows move across the wall. The prisoners have only ever seen shadows, so they call the shadows real things.

One prisoner is unchained and turned around. The fire hurts his eyes. He is dragged up out of the cave into daylight, and slowly he sees trees, animals and finally the sun itself. When he goes back to tell the others, they think he has gone mad.

Here is what Plato means. The things we see every day, chairs, horses, acts of kindness, are like the shadows. Behind them sit what he calls forms: the perfect pattern of a chair, of a horse, of kindness. The forms are the real things, and you reach them by thinking, not by looking.

So for Plato, the world your eyes show you is a copy. The original is somewhere your eyes cannot go.
cards.simpler: Plato tells this story in the Republic. Prisoners sit chained in a cave, facing a wall. A fire behind them throws puppet shadows onto the wall. The prisoners have only seen shadows, so they call them real. One prisoner is freed, climbs into daylight and sees the sun. Plato's point: **everyday things are like those shadows**. Behind them sit perfect patterns he calls forms, and those are the real things. You reach forms by thinking, not by looking.

cards.prompt: In the cave story, what stands for the everyday world you see with your eyes?

whyNot.b: That's the forms, not the seen world: the sun is the highest truth the freed prisoner reaches by leaving the cave.
whyNot.c: That's what keeps the prisoners facing the wall, Plato's picture of habit and never questioning, not the world itself.

cards.reteach: Plato's whole point is that what we see is secondhand. A shadow is made by a real object but is not the object. He says the chairs and horses in front of you are shadows of their perfect forms in the same way.

cards.title: The triangle on the napkin
cards.body:
Draw a triangle on a napkin and measure its 3 angles with a protractor. You will get something like 179 or 181 degrees, never exactly 180, because pencil lines have width and your hand shakes.

Plato says: the true triangle, whose angles add to exactly 180, exists only as a form. Your napkin drawing is a shadow of it, and you know the 180 rule by thinking, not by measuring.

Aristotle says: there is no second triangle floating somewhere else. The shape is in the drawings. Look at 50 of them, notice what they all share, and that shared pattern is all a triangle ever was.
cards.simpler: Draw a triangle on a napkin and measure its three angles. You get 179 or 181 degrees, never exactly 180, because hands shake. Plato says the true triangle, whose angles add to exactly 180, exists only as a form. Your drawing is its shadow, and you know the 180 rule by thinking. Aristotle says **there is no second triangle somewhere else**. Look at 50 drawings, notice what they share, and that shared shape is all a triangle ever was.

cards.title: Aristotle turns around
cards.body:
Aristotle studied under Plato in Athens for about 20 years, then set up his own school. His reply was blunt: there is no separate world of forms. The pattern of a horse is in the horses. Want to know what a horse is? Go and look at horses, lots of them.

He lived this. He cracked open hen's eggs on different days to watch how the chick forms, and he wrote long descriptions sorting animals into groups. His method was: observe closely, compare many cases, then state the general rule.

That is roughly what a scientist does today, so a scientist is closer to Aristotle. But Plato has not left the table. When a physicist trusts a clean formula over a messy reading from the lab, saying the instrument must be off, that is a Platonic move: the perfect law is more real than the noisy measurement.
cards.simpler: After about 20 years with Plato, Aristotle opened his own school and said there is no separate world of forms. **The pattern of a horse is in the horses**, so go look at horses. He cracked open hen's eggs on different days to watch chicks grow, and sorted animals into groups. Look closely, compare many cases, state the rule. A scientist today works this way. But a physicist who trusts a clean formula over messy lab readings is making Plato's move.

cards.prompt: A doctor wants to know what a healthy resting heart rate is. She records the heart rates of 200 healthy people and reports the range most of them fall in. Whose method is this?

options.text: Plato's, because she is looking for the perfect heart rate behind all the messy readings
Socrates', because she is questioning what people believe about health
Aristotle's, because she finds the pattern by looking at many real cases

whyNot.a: That's Plato's direction, not hers: he would reach the ideal by thinking, not by counting 200 pulses.
whyNot.b: That's Socrates' method from chapter 2, asking why about a belief. She is not questioning anyone, she is measuring.

cards.reteach: Ask one question: did the person get the answer by looking at many things, or by reasoning towards an ideal they could never see? Looking at many things is Aristotle. Reasoning towards the unseen ideal is Plato.

cards.body: People hear the cave story and say Plato thought the everyday world is fake or does not exist. He did not. Shadows are real shadows, cast by real objects. His claim is that the seen world is real but lesser, a copy of something more perfect. Spot the mistake when someone says Plato thought nothing we see is real. That is too strong by half.
cards.simpler: People hear the cave story and say Plato thought the everyday world is fake or does not exist. He did not think that. Shadows are real shadows, thrown by real objects. His claim is that **the world we see is real but lesser**, a copy of something more perfect, like a photo of a face. So when someone says Plato thought nothing we see is real, that is the mistake. It goes too far.

cards.prompt: Plato and Aristotle disagree about one thing in this chapter. Which?

options.text: Whether you should question your beliefs by asking why
Where the true pattern of a thing is found: beyond things by thinking, or inside things by looking
Whether a drawn triangle can ever measure exactly 180 degrees

whyNot.a: That's Socrates' habit from chapter 2, and both men kept it. Neither argued against asking why.
whyNot.c: That's the detail from the napkin example, and both agree the drawing is never exact. They differ on where the exact triangle lives.

cards.reteach: Picture one horse. Plato says its horse-ness lives somewhere beyond it, and this animal is a rough copy. Aristotle says horse-ness is right here, in this animal and the others like it. Beyond or inside: that is the whole disagreement.

cards.body: Pick up your cup. Ask out loud: is the cup-ness in this cup, or is this cup a rough copy of a perfect cup I can only think about? Say which man you just sided with.
cards.simpler: Pick up your cup and ask out loud: **is the cup-ness inside this cup**, or is this cup a rough copy of a perfect cup that you can only think about? If you said the cup-ness is in the cup, you sided with Aristotle. If you said the cup is a copy of a perfect one, you sided with Plato. Say which man you just agreed with.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now tell the cave story in 3 sentences and say whether a scientist works more like Plato or Aristotle.
